exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON PK Fc {freq} Hz Gain {gain} dB Q {q}

peaking-eq.commonConfusion: Not a shelf (which tilts everything above/below a point) and not a graphic EQ slider (fixed center frequencies).
peaking-eq.whenToUse: Fix a resonant note, add presence, or carve space between instruments.
peaking-eq.name: Peaking EQ (bell)
peaking-eq.summary: Boost or cut a band of frequencies around a center point.
peaking-eq.plainMeaning: A bell-shaped boost or cut centered on a frequency you choose. Narrow Q affects fewer neighbors; wide Q is gentler and broader.
peaking-eq.history: Grew out of 1970s parametric equalizers (e.g. George Massenburg) that let engineers sweep frequency, gain, and bandwidth continuously instead of fixed graphic bands.

exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON LPQ Fc {freq} Hz Q {q}

low-pass.commonConfusion: Low-pass removes highs; high-pass removes lows. Names describe what they pass, not what they cut.
low-pass.whenToUse: Tame harshness, hide noise, or keep a bass part from competing with cymbals.
low-pass.name: Low-pass (high-cut)
low-pass.summary: Lets lows through; attenuates highs above the cutoff.
low-pass.plainMeaning: Frequencies above the cutoff are reduced. Steeper slopes remove highs more aggressively.
low-pass.history: Classic analog synthesis and loudspeaker crossover building block; ‘high-cut’ is the mix-desk name for the same idea.

exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON HPQ Fc {freq} Hz Q {q}

high-pass.commonConfusion: People say ‘roll off the lows’ meaning high-pass, not low-pass.
high-pass.whenToUse: Clean mic stands, HVAC rumble, and unused low end before mixing.
high-pass.name: High-pass (low-cut)
high-pass.summary: Lets highs through; attenuates lows below the cutoff.
high-pass.plainMeaning: Cuts rumble and low mud while keeping the rest of the signal. Every vocal and many mics start here.
high-pass.history: Recording-console channel strips standardized low-cut switches long before DAW plugins; slopes often 6–24 dB/oct.

exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON LSC Fc {freq} Hz Gain {gain} dB

low-shelf.commonConfusion: A shelf changes a whole region; a peaking band is local.
low-shelf.whenToUse: Overall bass weight without surgically targeting one note.
low-shelf.name: Low shelf
low-shelf.summary: Boost or cut everything below a corner frequency by roughly the same amount.
low-shelf.plainMeaning: A gentle tilt of the bass region rather than a narrow bell. Think ‘more/less bass’ as a broad stroke.
low-shelf.history: Tone controls on hi-fi amps and mixing desks used shelving filters decades before parametric bells were common.

exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON HSC Fc {freq} Hz Gain {gain} dB

high-shelf.commonConfusion: Not the same as a high-pass (which removes lows).
high-shelf.whenToUse: Add sheen or reduce harshness across the top end.
high-shelf.name: High shelf
high-shelf.summary: Boost or cut everything above a corner frequency.
high-shelf.plainMeaning: Broad treble or ‘air’ control. Often used for polish rather than surgical fixes.
high-shelf.history: Companion to the bass shelf on classic tone stacks and console channel EQs.

exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON NO Fc {freq} Hz Q {q}

notch.commonConfusion: A notch is a cut; peaking EQ can boost or cut.
notch.whenToUse: Kill 50/60 Hz hum harmonics or a ringing room mode without gutting the tone.
notch.name: Notch (band-reject)
notch.summary: Deep, narrow cut at a center frequency.
notch.plainMeaning: Scoops out a thin slice—useful for hum, feedback, or a single bad resonance.
notch.history: Feedback destroyers and graphic notches in live sound popularized surgical reject filters.

exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON BP Fc {freq} Hz Q {q}

band-pass.commonConfusion: Band-pass keeps a band; band-reject (notch) removes one.
band-pass.whenToUse: Special effects or isolating a frequency region for analysis.
band-pass.name: Band-pass
band-pass.summary: Passes a mid band; attenuates below and above.
band-pass.plainMeaning: Only a slice of the spectrum remains—telephone effects, drum tuning, creative filtering.
band-pass.history: Standard second-order filter type in analog synthesis (alongside LP/HP/notch).

exports.equalizerApo: Filter: ON AP Fc {freq} Hz Q {q}

all-pass.commonConfusion: ‘All-pass’ does not mean ‘no effect’—phase still moves.
all-pass.whenToUse: Phase alignment, multi-way speakers, and modulation FX building blocks.
all-pass.name: All-pass
all-pass.summary: Keeps magnitude flat while shifting phase around a frequency.
all-pass.plainMeaning: You may not hear a solo all-pass as a tone change, but it rearranges phase—useful in crossovers and phasers.
all-pass.history: Critical in Linkwitz-Riley crossovers and analog phaser circuits.

q-bandwidth.commonConfusion: Q is not gain. Gain is how much; Q is how wide.
q-bandwidth.whenToUse: Decide whether a cut should be surgical or musical.
q-bandwidth.name: Q / bandwidth
q-bandwidth.summary: How wide or narrow an EQ band is.
q-bandwidth.plainMeaning: Higher Q = narrower bell. Bandwidth is the inverse idea expressed in octaves.
q-bandwidth.history: Q comes from resonant circuits in electronics; audio borrowed the same dimensionless ratio.

slope-db-oct.commonConfusion: Steeper is not always better—phase and resonance change too.
slope-db-oct.whenToUse: Choose gentle musical rolls vs surgical bricks.
slope-db-oct.name: Slope (dB/octave)
slope-db-oct.summary: How steeply a filter attenuates past the cutoff.
slope-db-oct.plainMeaning: Each doubling of frequency (one octave), level drops by N dB past the cutoff for an ideal slope description.
slope-db-oct.history: Filter order (1st, 2nd, 4th…) maps to 6 dB/oct steps in classic analog designs.

butterworth.commonConfusion: Butterworth vs Linkwitz-Riley: LR is often preferred for speaker crossovers because summed response is flat.
butterworth.whenToUse: When you want a clean, predictable roll-off without passband ripple.
butterworth.name: Butterworth
butterworth.summary: Maximally flat passband filter response family.
butterworth.plainMeaning: No ripple in the passband; common default for ‘transparent’ crossovers and HPFs.
butterworth.history: Named after Stephen Butterworth (1930 paper on filter amplifiers).

linkwitz-riley.commonConfusion: Not every DAW ‘crossover’ is true LR alignment.
linkwitz-riley.name: Linkwitz-Riley
linkwitz-riley.summary: Crossover filter alignment that sums flat on-axis.
linkwitz-riley.plainMeaning: Even-order Linkwitz-Riley is cascaded Butterworth sections (LR4 = two 2nd-order Butter stages). Lows and highs sum flat when each side uses the matching high/low pair.
linkwitz-riley.history: Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley; widely taught in DIY speaker and PA system design.

graphic-eq.whenToUse: Room tuning, feedback hunting, broad tonal shape.
graphic-eq.name: Graphic EQ
graphic-eq.plainMeaning: You see a ‘graphic’ of the curve as slider positions. Fast for live tuning; less precise than full parametric. This demo is a 10-band octave graphic.
graphic-eq.history: Live sound and consumer hi-fi popularized octave and 1/3-octave graphic equalizers.

linear-vs-minimum-phase.commonConfusion: Linear-phase is not ‘higher quality’ by default—trade latency and pre-echo.
linear-vs-minimum-phase.whenToUse: Mastering surgical cuts sometimes use linear-phase; tracking often prefers minimum-phase.
linear-vs-minimum-phase.name: Linear-phase vs minimum-phase
linear-vs-minimum-phase.summary: Two ways EQ can treat phase while changing frequency balance.
linear-vs-minimum-phase.plainMeaning: Minimum-phase (typical analog-style) shifts phase as it EQ’s. Linear-phase keeps phase relationships but can introduce pre-ringing and latency. This browser audition uses Web Audio biquads — minimum-phase only — so you can still feel the magnitude EQ while reading the phase trade-off.
linear-vs-minimum-phase.history: Digital EQ made linear-phase practical; analog desks were inherently minimum-phase.

cutoff.commonConfusion: Cutoff is not always where the sound ‘disappears’—slope still continues.
cutoff.whenToUse: Any LP/HP/shelf/crossover control labeled frequency or cutoff.
cutoff.name: Cutoff frequency
cutoff.summary: The corner where a filter begins its primary roll-off.
cutoff.plainMeaning: Usually defined at −3 dB for many classic filters.

resonance.commonConfusion: Resonance can self-oscillate on some designs—not the same as a gentle EQ Q.
resonance.whenToUse: Creative filter sweeps; use sparingly on mix EQ.
resonance.name: Resonance
resonance.summary: Emphasis near the cutoff, related to Q.
resonance.plainMeaning: On synth filters, resonance peaking at the cutoff creates the classic ‘wah’ or scream.
resonance.history: Moog and other subtractive synths made resonant low-pass iconic.

compressor.commonConfusion: Compression reduces dynamic range; limiting is a high-ratio special case.
compressor.whenToUse: Control peaks, glue a bus, or shape punch with attack/release.
compressor.name: Compressor
compressor.summary: Automatically reduces level when the signal exceeds a threshold.
compressor.plainMeaning: Turns down loud parts (and often adds makeup gain) so dynamics sit more evenly.
compressor.history: Broadcast and recording from the mid-20th century used leveling amplifiers (e.g. LA-2A, 1176) before digital plugins.

limiter.commonConfusion: A limiter still needs sensible threshold/ceiling—it is not magic headroom.
limiter.whenToUse: Catch peaks before clipping; mastering ceilings; live protection.
limiter.name: Limiter
limiter.summary: Compressor with a very high ratio that prevents exceeding a ceiling.
limiter.plainMeaning: A ‘brick wall’ (or soft) ceiling so peaks cannot pass a set level.
limiter.history: Broadcast transmitters and vinyl cutting required peak protection; brickwall limiters became mastering staples in the loudness era.

expander.commonConfusion: Expander ≠ compressor; watch the transfer curve direction.
expander.whenToUse: Reduce room noise between phrases without a hard gate chop.
expander.name: Expander
expander.summary: Increases dynamic range by turning down signals below a threshold.
expander.plainMeaning: Quiet parts get quieter—opposite direction of a compressor.
expander.history: Noise reduction and creative dynamics; related to gates.

gate.commonConfusion: Too-high threshold chops consonants and decays.
gate.whenToUse: Drum bleed, noisy amps, podcast room tone between words (carefully).
gate.name: Noise gate
gate.summary: Mutes or attenuates when level falls below a threshold.
gate.plainMeaning: When the signal is quiet enough, the gate closes. Attack/hold/release shape the open/close.
gate.history: Live drums and guitar amps used gates to kill bleed; still standard on console channels.

obs.note: OBS uses compressor sidechain / source ducking depending on version and filter setup

ducking.commonConfusion: Ducking is a use-case; the mechanism is usually sidechain compression or a dedicated duck module.
ducking.whenToUse: Podcasts, streams, ads—keep voice intelligible over beds.
ducking.name: Ducking
ducking.summary: One signal’s level automatically turns another down.
ducking.plainMeaning: Music ducks under speech: when the voice is present, the bed gets quieter, then recovers.
ducking.history: Radio voice-over and broadcast production; sidechain compression popularized the effect in dance music.

sidechain.commonConfusion: Sidechain is the control path, not a genre.
sidechain.name: Sidechain
sidechain.summary: A detector path that listens to a different signal than the one being processed.
sidechain.plainMeaning: The compressor (or gate) watches signal B to control signal A—classic kick-ducks-bass.
sidechain.history: Hardware compressors offered key/sidechain inputs; EDM made ‘sidechain’ a household word.

threshold.commonConfusion: Threshold alone does nothing without ratio/range.
threshold.whenToUse: Set how much of the signal engages the processor.
threshold.name: Threshold
threshold.summary: Level where dynamics processing starts acting.
threshold.plainMeaning: Above (compressor) or below (gate/expander) this level, the device changes gain.
threshold.history: Standard control on leveling amps and VCA compressors.

ratio.name: Ratio
ratio.summary: How strongly levels above threshold are reduced.
ratio.plainMeaning: 4:1 means 4 dB over threshold becomes 1 dB at the output (idealized).
ratio.history: VCA and FET compressor front panels standardized ratio switches.

attack-release.commonConfusion: Fast everything can sound pumpy or distorted; context matters.
attack-release.whenToUse: Preserve transients (slower attack) or catch them (fast attack).
attack-release.name: Attack / release
attack-release.summary: How fast processing engages and recovers.
attack-release.plainMeaning: Attack: how quickly gain reduction starts. Release: how quickly it returns.
attack-release.history: Timing constants define the ‘character’ of classic compressors as much as the gain cell.

knee.commonConfusion: Knee is not the same as ratio.
knee.whenToUse: Soft for transparent vocals; hard for assertive leveling.
knee.name: Knee
knee.summary: Whether compression onset is abrupt (hard) or gradual (soft).
knee.plainMeaning: Soft knee starts reducing gain before the exact threshold for a smoother transition.
knee.history: Described in compressor manuals as hard vs soft knee curves.

makeup-gain.commonConfusion: Makeup can fool you into thinking ‘more compression = better’ because louder wins.
makeup-gain.whenToUse: Match perceived loudness when A/B’ing bypass.
makeup-gain.name: Makeup gain
makeup-gain.summary: Output gain to compensate for compression reduction.
makeup-gain.plainMeaning: After turning peaks down, boost the whole signal so loudness matches again.
makeup-gain.history: Always present on hardware compressors so comparative leveling was possible.

parallel-compression.commonConfusion: Requires a send/blend; not just ‘more ratio’ on one insert.
parallel-compression.whenToUse: Drums, vocals, mix bus density without killing punch.
parallel-compression.name: Parallel compression
parallel-compression.summary: Blend a heavily compressed copy under the dry signal.
parallel-compression.plainMeaning: Keep transients from the dry path while adding body from a squashed parallel path.
parallel-compression.history: Associated with NYC mix engineers; also called Motown-style parallel techniques in drum rooms.

multiband-dynamics.commonConfusion: More bands ≠ better; crossovers can smear if overused.
multiband-dynamics.name: Multiband dynamics
multiband-dynamics.summary: Split the spectrum and compress/limit each band separately.
multiband-dynamics.plainMeaning: Control boom without dulling highs, or tame harshness without thinning lows.
multiband-dynamics.history: Broadcast processors and mastering chains adopted multiband limiting heavily.

upward-compression.commonConfusion: Not the same as makeup gain alone.
upward-compression.whenToUse: Dialogue consistency without squashing peaks as hard.
upward-compression.name: Upward compression
upward-compression.summary: Raises quieter signals toward a target instead of only cutting peaks.
upward-compression.plainMeaning: Brings up detail under a ceiling rather than only suppressing loud bits.
upward-compression.history: Discussed in modern digital processors and some vintage leveling philosophies.

delay.commonConfusion: Delay is discrete repeats; reverb is dense reflections.
delay.whenToUse: Space, rhythm, and depth in mixes.
delay.name: Delay
delay.summary: Echo repeats after a set time.
delay.plainMeaning: Echo repeats after a set time.
delay.history: Studio effects evolved from tape loops, plates, chambers, and digital algorithms into plugin standards.

slapback.whenToUse: Space, rhythm, and depth in mixes.
slapback.name: Slapback delay
slapback.summary: Single short echo familiar from 1950s rockabilly.
slapback.plainMeaning: Single short echo familiar from 1950s rockabilly.
slapback.history: Studio effects evolved from tape loops, plates, chambers, and digital algorithms into plugin standards.
